title: Why do Iberian household power bills diverge when wholesale electricity prices converge?
summary: Spain and Portugal come close to operating one wholesale electricity market, yet a household on either side of the border can experience a common energy shock quite differently. The joint research by Banco de España and Banco de Portugal economists traces a similar distinction in trade, labour and finance. Goods producers and banks have substantial cross-border links. A firm selling services, a graduate looking for work or a household buying electricity still faces national institutions. The strength of one connection is a poor guide to how far a shock will travel through another.

The wholesale power evidence is unusually direct. From 2015 to 2025 the Spanish and Portuguese day-ahead prices were within €1 per megawatt-hour in about 95% of hours. The comparable share at the Spanish–French border was about 30%. When the interconnector can accommodate the scheduled flow, an extra unit of demand in one bidding zone can be met by generation in the other. The hours when the price separates matter too. A high fraction of hours with similar prices says little by itself about the size of the spread in the remaining hours or the cost of meeting demand during a shortage.

For households the relevant price is the tariff on their bill. In the second half of 2022 household electricity cost about €0.335 per kilowatt-hour in Spain and €0.222 in Portugal. The paper reports increases of roughly 40% and 2%, respectively, compared with the second half of 2019. The comparison draws attention to the role of retail contracts, regulation and the timing with which wholesale costs reach customers. An analyst using Iberian wholesale prices alone to project household purchasing power would miss this divergence. The price comparison establishes its scale. It does not isolate the effect of any one tariff provision.

Trade shows why sharing a currency and a border also leaves room for further integration. The authors infer bilateral trade frictions equivalent to a tariff of around 20% in manufacturing and more than 100% in services. These are model estimates of the obstacles needed to account for the trade pattern. They cannot be read as a tax that a government could repeal. In a structural counterfactual, reducing the implicit bilateral trade costs by a quarter raises the level of real GDP by 0.17% in Portugal and 0.06% in Spain. Halving them yields gains of 0.39% and 0.13%. The asymmetry matters to an investor comparing two economies exposed to the same reform. Those level changes are conditional on the model and supply no implementation timetable.

Other channels qualify an account centred on merchandise exports. Movement of workers and students between the two countries is limited relative to other neighbouring European economies. The clearest financial links run through banks, while direct and portfolio investment do less to set the pair apart. Cross-border banking can transmit a funding or credit disturbance even where labour is slow to move. Its importance in the balance-sheet data cannot reveal in advance whether a bank would absorb a local credit shock or reduce lending elsewhere. For an assessment of Iberian risk, the paper therefore points to different observables for each question: hourly wholesale spreads for physical congestion, retail bills for household exposure, sectoral trade for market access and bank balance sheets for financial transmission.

questions.question: When does a shared wholesale price become a shared household inflation shock?
questions.detail: Following the same wholesale shock, compare effective tariffs as retail contracts reset. A persistent cross-country gap among customers with similar contracts would direct attention to taxes, network charges or support arrangements. A gap that closes after renewal would put more weight on contract timing. Distribution across households matters for the purchasing-power effect.

questions.question: How much of the residual energy risk is concentrated in a few hours?
questions.detail: Measure the size and duration of Spanish–Portuguese spreads in hours outside the €1 threshold. Then examine whether those hours coincide with high demand or constrained cross-border capacity. A small number of expensive hours could matter considerably to a purchaser with unhedged peak demand even if annual price convergence is very high.

questions.question: What could turn the modelled trade gains into observable changes?
questions.detail: Identify a specific service barrier, the firms facing it and the date at which it changes. Compare market entry, bilateral sales and prices in the exposed activity with a similar activity where the barrier remained. That supplies a test of the reduced-cost mechanism and of how quickly any gains reach households.

questions.question: Would cross-border banks cushion a national shock or amplify it?
questions.detail: Trace which group entity supplies funding and which holds the affected loans. Credit growth at Portuguese and Spanish affiliates after a common shock could reflect demand, funding reallocation or a change in underwriting. Borrower-level comparisons alongside group funding costs would help distinguish these explanations.

limitation: The November date is the date on Banco de España’s English publication page. The Spanish catalogue carried the study in October. The paper reports structural comparisons and model scenarios, without identifying an announcement-window market reaction.
